paragraphs.text: At the University of Halden, a team led by biologist Ingrid Moe has spent four years studying how tomato plants respond to a lack of water. Plants cannot move away when conditions become difficult, but they are far from passive.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: When the soil begins to dry, the roots send a chemical signal to the leaves. The leaves then close the tiny openings on their surface, called stomata, which reduces the amount of water lost to the air. This happens long before the plant shows any visible sign of stress, such as drooping.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Moe’s team found that thirsty plants also produce faint clicking sounds as air bubbles form inside their stems. Using sensitive microphones placed ten centimetres away, the researchers recorded up to 35 clicks per hour from plants that had not been watered for five days, compared with almost none from well-watered plants.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The team believes the sounds could help farmers. A small device in a greenhouse could listen to the crop and switch on the irrigation only when plants are actually short of water, rather than on a fixed timetable. A trial of such a system is planned for next year.
paragraphs.label: D
